summary: Mars Colony Survival is a free 3D browser game where kids aged 7–12 run an outpost in Valles Marineris, the real Grand Canyon of Mars, and learn that no choice is free. The world is built from NASA's THEMIS map of the canyon, and the title globe streams live from NASA Mars Trek. Players gather real Martian minerals (basalt, magnetite, gypsum, sulfur, olivine and water ice), make water, oxygen and food, and grow a tiny base into Mars City across 29 missions. Random dust storms, solar radiation storms and equipment failures pause the game with two choices that both cost something: clean dusty solar panels outside and risk injury, or shut down rooms and save batteries; repair a broken oxygen unit, or burn oxygen candles with a fire risk. Every choice changes power, oxygen, food, equipment and a Colony Safety score, and each emergency card names the real NASA event behind it, such as Opportunity's 2018 dust storm. This turns real mission trade-offs into decisions kids can feel, not just facts to memorize. It runs on any device, works offline, needs no download or account, and Unlimited Lives lets kids fail, learn and try again.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Mars Colony Survival is a free 3D browser game where kids aged 7–12 manage a Martian outpost in Valles Marineris and experience the real trade-offs that astronauts and mission planners face. The player is the first astronaut of a small base. With the robot ROVER-B, they explore the canyon, gather real Martian minerals, mine ice, produce water, oxygen and food, and grow the base into a self-sustaining Mars City across 29 missions in 5 chapters. A Handbook always shows the next objective in plain language: what to collect, build, upgrade and equip.

HOW THE TRADE-OFFS WORK
No choice is free. Each resource has a real cost, and emergencies arrive at random times, so every playthrough is different. When one hits, the game pauses and offers two choices that both cost something:
- Power: dust builds up on the solar panels and cuts power. In a dust storm, risk an outdoor repair (injury and equipment risk) or shut down rooms and run on batteries (the greenhouse may get cold).
- Life support: when the MOXIE oxygen unit fails, repair it with spare parts (it may fail) or burn oxygen candles (fire risk).
- Radiation shielding: during a solar radiation storm, shelter in the station or a cave and stop working, or stay outside with a radiation visor that replaces your head lamp.
- Food: when the greenhouse heater fails, spend energy to heat it, or let the plants go dormant and risk losing the crop.
- Earth is far: supply landers take time, and correcting a drifting lander costs power and water.
Every decision changes resources, energy, equipment condition and a Colony Safety score that reduces future damage. The Mission Log records every choice and its result, and each emergency card names the real event behind it (Opportunity 2018, Spirit 2009, Mir 1997, MOXIE, ISS water recycling).

REAL NASA DATA
- The whole map is NASA's THEMIS mosaic of Valles Marineris (Mars Odyssey), embedded in the game and rebuilt as 3D terrain. The relief is reconstructed from the image and exaggerated for play.
- The title-screen globe streams live tiles from the NASA Mars Trek WMTS API (Viking colour mosaic).
- Minerals, rooms, events and 20 Science Notes come from NASA mission results: Curiosity (sulfur crystals, radiation of about 0.7 mSv per day), Opportunity (hematite "blueberries", iron meteorite, the 2018 dust storm), Spirit, Phoenix (buried ice), Perseverance (MOXIE, sounds of Mars, sample tubes) and ISS life support (about 98% water recovery, Veggie, Kilopower).
- NASA DONKI shaped the solar-storm warnings, and OSDR research on bone and muscle loss in low gravity shaped crew health. These two are design references and are not live data yet.
- Sources are credited inside the game: on the title screen, in the map panel and on every emergency card.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Kids learn the decision-making logic behind a mission, not just its outcome. Teachers get a free classroom tool with no download or account. It works offline on low-end laptops and phones. Three life modes (One Life, Five Lives, Unlimited Lives) let kids learn from failure without feeling punished, and older siblings and parents can explore the deeper tech tree.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES
HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript; three.js (WebGL) for 3D; Canvas 2D to decode NASA imagery; the NASA Mars Trek WMTS API; Web Audio API for live-synthesized music and sound effects (no audio files); browser localStorage for autosave. Tested with automated play-throughs in headless Chrome (Playwright) at desktop and phone sizes: all 29 missions reach victory. The game is one self-contained file of about 770 KB, with no server.

CREATIVITY
The world is a real NASA map, every emergency is a real mission event, and every decision is a genuine trade-off. Outdoor sounds are muffled, the way Perseverance's microphones recorded the thin Martian air. An original synthwave score changes mood for exploring, building, danger and victory.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Plain language for young players; no "safe" choice without a cost; honest labelling of live versus embedded data; low barrier to entry (browser, offline, no account); accessibility (touch controls, three graphics levels); no copyrighted music or images; no NASA logos or branding.

NEXT STEPS
Connect live NASA DONKI solar activity to in-game radiation warnings, add a true radio-delay mechanic for messages to Earth, build a simpler kid mode with three core resources and a picture glossary, and release an Arabic version with a teacher guide.
